 Kerry Hannon · Senior Columnist Sat, October 31, 2026 at 1:21 PM MDT 5 min read The window to sign up for 2027 healthcare coverage under the Affordable Care Act opens Sunday in most states.   
 With healthcare costs a top concern for Americans already slammed by sticky inflation, this year's enrollment — running through Dec. 15 to get a plan that starts Jan. 1 — comes at a time when monthly premiums are climbing and insurers are shutting plans.  
 For 2027, average full-price premiums on federal and state-run marketplace plans are set to increase by roughly 13%, according to a new KFF analysis published on Friday. Most price hikes across the country range from 10% to 20%.  
 States that run their own enrollment platforms are seeing premium increases of 16%, per the researchers.  
 The increases are being driven by a rise in overall medical care costs, inflation, and labor shortages. 
 "Automatically renewing your current coverage before looking at alternatives is a big mistake," Louise Norris, a health policy analyst for healthinsurance.org, told Yahoo Finance.  
 This will be the second year in a row of double-digit increases. For many people, 2026 ACA premiums jumped more than 20% and higher earners lost premium subsidies entirely. 
 Where you live impacts what you pay 
 Premium hikes vary widely from state to state. In Vermont, for example, there is likely to be an average increase of 3% compared to an average hike of almost 28% in Arizona. 
 In about half the states, the plans available are from the same insurance companies in 2027 as they were in 2026. 
 But those plans could be changing in terms of what they cover, what providers are in the network, what drugs are covered, the deductible amount, and the out-of-pocket maximum. Those are the sorts of things that change every year, Norris said. 
 And there are quite a few folks whose 2026 plan is not available for renewal next year. In 26 states, at least one insurer is leaving the marketplace.  
 "If it's your plan, it's a big issue to you," she added. 
 As of this past week, 11 carriers have announced that they will exit the ACA marketplaces, either in some or all states. Cigna, which has more than 350,000 ACA enrollees, will exit all 11 states where it offers ACA plans.  
 "We did not make this decision lightly and appreciate the importance of ensuring patients have continuity through the transition, and we will support members through their open enrollment transitions into 2027," Brian Evanko, Cigna Group's president and CEO, said in an earnings call. "This is a small business for us today, and it's been shrinking in recent years." 
 Story Continues Looking ahead to 2027, several insurers have said they "expect the market to continue to deteriorate in 2027 as a continued result of the enhanced premium tax credits ending," according to KFF. 
 How it works 
 Marketplace plans are divided into four tiers . Bronze plans are typically the most affordable with the lowest premiums, but have the highest deductibles (the amount you pay for covered medical costs before insurance kicks in). Platinum plans tend to have the highest premiums, but lower out-of-pocket costs. 
 Catastrophic health plans have low monthly premiums and high deductibles. If you're age 30 and older, however, you'll generally need a hardship or affordability exemption to purchase the coverage .  
 Underneath the top-line premium and deductible amounts, the coverage you receive under different plans is all over the map. Some cover certain hospitals, physicians, and drugs, or provide a range of deductibles and co-payments.  
 There are two main types of financial breaks available to marketplace enrollees. The first type, called the premium tax credit, reduces enrollees' monthly insurance premiums. Premium tax credits can be applied to marketplace plans in any level of coverage. 
 The second type of financial aid, the cost-sharing reduction (CSR), reduces your deductibles and other out-of-pocket costs when you go to the doctor or have a hospital stay. You can only receive CSR financial aid if you enroll in a silver-level plan and meet the specific income requirements (typically between 100% and 250% of the Federal Poverty Level). 
 There are also state-funded subsidies in several states .  
 Health insurance subsidies 
 Most marketplace enrollees are eligible for premium subsidies, even after Congress allowed federal subsidy enhancements to expire at the end of 2025. 
 "There will be increases in premiums, although most enrollees who qualify for subsidies may be fully or partly protected," said Rayna Wallace, a KFF policy analyst. 
 Those who don't qualify will feel it. For a 40-year-old non-smoking adult who is not eligible for subsidies and enrolls in a bronze plan, the premium payment climbed from $381 per month in 2025 to $511 per month in 2027, she said. "The two-year increase in premiums for this individual is profound — a 34% increase." 
 Of the nearly 23.1 million people who selected plans through the exchanges during the open enrollment period for 2026, 20 million were receiving premium subsidies, according to data from the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services . 
 Most of those people will continue to qualify for a subsidy next year, assuming they haven't had a big increase in income, but the coverage is likely to still be expensive for many people, Norris said. 
 Where to get help 
 KFF provides a calculator to run your numbers to see if you qualify for a subsidy. Another calculator can be found on healthinsurance.org. 
 If you're switching plans for 2027, it's crucial to make sure your doctors are in-network before you sign up. "If you don't actively choose another plan, you may be automatically re-enrolled in a different plan that may not suit your needs," said Wallace. 
 You might even want to consult a licensed broker, or check out the resources listed on the marketplace website for help. 
 Kerry Hannon is a Senior Columnist at Yahoo Finance. She is a career and retirement strategist and the author of 14 books, including " Retirement Bites: A Gen X Guide to Securing Your Financial Future, " " In Control at 50+: How to Succeed in the New World of Work ," and "Never Too Old to Get Rich."
